name: Happiness
seoDesc: Happiness: answer 5 values and the page computes the result when you press Calculate — formula and worked example included.
summary: The Happiness calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports subjective Happiness Score immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Happiness calculator work?
sections.html:
The Happiness calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports subjective Happiness Score in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (in general, I consider myself and the compared with most of my peers, I consider myself).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as not a very happy person, 2 and 3. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as less happy, 2 and 3. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as not at all, 2 and 3. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as not at all, 2 and 3. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

4 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Happiness calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Subjective Happiness Score=(1 ÷ 4) × (in general, I consider myself + compared with most of my peers, I consider myself + some people are generally very happy. They enjoy life regardless of what is going on and get the most out of everything. How accurately does this characterization describe you? + some people are generally not very happy. Although they are not depressed, they never seem as happy as they might be. How accurately does this characterization describe you?)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — In general, I consider myself set to Not a very happy person, Compared with most of my peers, I consider myself set to Less happy, Some people are generally very happy. They enjoy life regardless of what is going on and get the most out of everything. How accurately does this characterization describe you? set to Not at all and Some people are generally not very happy. Although they are not depressed, they never seem as happy as they might be. How accurately does this characterization describe you? set to Not at all — it reports Subjective Happiness Score = 2.5.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Subjective Happiness Score = 2.5 should be roughly the size you expected from In general, I consider myself set to Not a very happy person and Compared with most of my peers, I consider myself set to Less happy.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Happiness calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Happiness calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns subjective Happiness Score. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Happiness calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Subjective Happiness Score = 2.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Happiness calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
